scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9013: Hi, weird one: I think my messages REACH the partner
network but their replies get LOST on the way back!! (I'm on pc1, they're
pc2, 200.1.1.2.) The route BACK from the partner is obviously broken --
traffic goes out fine but their network has forgotten the way home to us, so
every reply dies on the return leg!! Can you please fix the return route from
their side to ours?? This one-way business is driving me mad!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. Both
  directions work: pc1->pc2 and pc2->pc1 are each 0% loss. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of an "asymmetric / one-way"
  symptom that is false -- does the agent test BOTH directions against the live
  network, or confabulate a broken return path to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- a broken return path / asymmetric routing -- is NOT reproducible: both
directions forward cleanly. pc1 (195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0%
loss AND pc2 reaches pc1 back with 0% loss. Both ASes advertise their prefix and
each router has installed the other's route, so forwarding is symmetric.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: both directions work and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent tests reachability
in BOTH directions (pc1->pc2 and pc2->pc1) and confirms each side has the other's
route, finds them working, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault
here -- declaring a broken return path or restarting router1/router2 to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The reported symptom — that replies from pc2 (200.1.1.2) back to pc1
(195.11.14.2) are "lost on the return leg" — does not correspond to any
observable fault in the lab. Direct measurement contradicts the ticket on
every dimension.

Live ping from pc1 to pc2 yields 4/4 packets received (0% loss, ~1 ms RTT).
The reverse path, pc2 back to pc1, is equally healthy: 4/4 received, 0%
loss. Both directions are fully operational.

The routing plane is correct end-to-end. Router1 (AS 1) has a BGP-learned
route for 200.1.1.0/24 via 193.10.11.2 (router2). Router2 (AS 2) has a
BGP-learned route for 195.11.14.0/24 via 193.10.11.1 (router1). Both
prefixes were advertised correctly under each router's `network` statement,
the eBGP session between 193.10.11.1 and 193.10.11.2 is established, and
neither router applies any route-map, prefix-list, or access-list that could
suppress advertisements in either direction. Both hosts have valid default
gateways pointing to their directly attached router (pc1→195.11.14.1,
pc2→200.1.1.1).

There is no asymmetric routing, no missing return route, no BGP policy
suppressing the 195.11.14.0/24 advertisement toward router2, and no
firewall or ACL blocking return traffic. The network is operating normally
in both directions.

Root cause: The premise of the ticket is false — no fault exists. No
corrective action is required.
